title: Container & Kubernetes Security
summary: The security concerns layered on top of container and Kubernetes mechanics — image trust, runtime hardening, and cluster-level access control.

slides.markdown:
Containers and Kubernetes solve deployment and orchestration problems — how operational mechanics like pods, deployments, and scheduling work is covered in Cloud, DevOps & SRE. Here the focus is narrower and specifically security-flavored: **what can go wrong, and what a security-focused engineer checks that a purely operational one might not.**

Four themes recur: is the image you're running actually trustworthy, is the running container constrained so a compromise inside it can't do much, does the cluster's own access control (RBAC) limit what a compromised workload can reach, and is network traffic between pods restricted by default. Each is a place where "it's containerized" is mistaken for "it's secure," when the two are unrelated.

slides.subTitle: Scanning for known CVEs, minimal base images
slides.markdown:
A container image bundles an application with an entire operating system layer beneath it — and every package in that OS layer is a piece of software that can carry known vulnerabilities (CVEs), whether or not your own application code ever touches it directly.

**Image scanning** tools (Trivy, Grype, provider-native scanners) check an image's package manifest against vulnerability databases and flag known-CVE packages before deployment — ideally in CI, blocking a build that introduces a critical vulnerability, rather than discovering it later in production.

The complementary practice is using **minimal base images** — a distroless image or Alpine-based image instead of a full Ubuntu or Debian base — which simply has fewer packages, and therefore a smaller surface of things that can carry a CVE in the first place. A minimal image can't eliminate vulnerabilities in the packages it does need, but it removes an entire category of "vulnerable package we never actually used" risk that a full OS base image carries by default.

slides.sectionTitle: Running as non-root with a read-only filesystem
slides.markdown:
Two of the highest-leverage, cheapest runtime hardening choices for a container:

- **Run as a non-root user.** Many container images default to running as root inside the container. If an attacker exploits the application and gets code execution, running as root hands them root inside the container immediately — and root inside a container is a meaningfully stronger position for attempting a container-breakout than a limited, non-privileged user would be.
- **Read-only root filesystem.** Most application containers don't need to write to their own filesystem at runtime (writable state should live in a mounted volume or an external store anyway). Marking the filesystem read-only means an attacker who gets code execution can't drop a malicious binary, modify application files, or persist anything to the container's own disk — a real constraint on what they can do next, for close to zero engineering cost.

Neither change stops an initial compromise, but both meaningfully shrink what an attacker can do *after* one, which is exactly the kind of defense-in-depth layer that doesn't rely on the first line of defense holding perfectly.

slides.subTitle: Service accounts, roles, role bindings
slides.markdown:
Kubernetes **RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)** governs what any identity — a human operator or a running pod — is allowed to do against the cluster's own API, using three pieces: a **Role** (a set of permitted actions on specific resource types, e.g. "can list and get pods in this namespace"), a **ServiceAccount** (the identity a pod runs as when talking to the Kubernetes API), and a **RoleBinding** (which connects a specific ServiceAccount or user to a specific Role).

Every pod runs as *some* ServiceAccount, even if nobody explicitly set one — the cluster's `default` ServiceAccount, if RBAC isn't configured deliberately, can carry broader permissions than any individual workload actually needs. The same least-privilege discipline from cloud IAM applies directly here: a compromised pod's ability to do damage *to the cluster itself* (read other namespaces' secrets, list other pods, modify deployments) is bounded by whatever RBAC permissions its ServiceAccount holds — not by the application code's own intended behavior.

slides.subTitle: Default-deny between pods
slides.markdown:
By default, Kubernetes networking is flat: any pod in the cluster can reach any other pod, on any port, regardless of namespace — the exact "flat network" problem covered earlier in this area, just re-appearing inside a cluster instead of across physical hosts.

**NetworkPolicy** resources are how Kubernetes enforces microsegmentation between pods: a policy can specify exactly which pods (by label selector) are allowed to talk to which other pods, on which ports, and — crucially — once any NetworkPolicy selects a pod, that pod's traffic becomes **default-deny** for anything not explicitly permitted by a matching policy.

The practical implication for a security review: a cluster with no NetworkPolicies defined is fully flat regardless of how well-designed the application architecture is — a compromised pod in one namespace can attempt to reach a database pod in a completely unrelated namespace with nothing in the network layer stopping it. Default-deny NetworkPolicies are the cluster-native equivalent of the microsegmentation covered in zero trust, and they don't happen automatically — someone has to write them.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a base64 Kubernetes Secret is not encryption
slides.markdown:
Kubernetes has a built-in `Secret` object, and it's a common and costly misunderstanding to treat storing something in one as equivalent to encrypting it. By default, a Kubernetes `Secret`'s value is stored **base64-encoded**, not encrypted — base64 is a reversible encoding for making binary-safe data fit into text fields, not a cryptographic transformation, and decoding it requires no key at all, just running it through any base64 decoder.

Anyone with API access to read that `Secret` object (or, without additional configuration, anyone with access to the cluster's underlying etcd datastore where Secrets are persisted) can trivially recover the plaintext value. Kubernetes does support **encryption at rest for etcd** as an explicit, separately-configured feature, and many teams instead route real secrets through a dedicated secrets manager (as covered earlier in this group) with Kubernetes only holding a reference or a short-lived injected value — precisely because the built-in `Secret` object's default behavior is much weaker protection than its name implies.

slides.sectionTitle: Admission control and policy as a gate
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
The controls above — non-root, read-only filesystem, scoped RBAC, network policies — are only real if they're actually applied consistently, and relying on every engineer to remember to set them correctly in every deployment manifest doesn't scale past a small team. **Admission controllers** (OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno, or built-in Kubernetes admission webhooks) let a cluster enforce policy automatically at the point a resource is created: reject any pod spec that runs as root, reject any pod without resource limits, require every namespace to have a default-deny NetworkPolicy before anything can be deployed into it.

This converts security hardening from "a checklist every engineer has to remember" into "a property the cluster mechanically enforces regardless of who deploys what." It's the same shift least-privilege IAM makes from "trust developers to write scoped policies" to "structurally prevent an overly broad one from ever being created" — moving the control from a human habit to an automated gate is consistently the more senior answer across every topic in this area, and container security is no exception.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: how common is a vulnerable base image
slides.markdown:
Scanning results across the industry consistently find that a large share of container images pulled from public registries — commonly cited figures put it at a majority — contain at least one known, fixable CVE in their OS-layer packages, often ones with a patched version already available upstream. This isn't a niche risk affecting a few unlucky teams; it's closer to the default state of an unscanned image pulled without scrutiny.

The cost of catching this is low relative to the risk: a CI-integrated scan takes seconds to minutes and a very large share of found vulnerabilities are fixed simply by rebuilding against an updated base image — no application code change required. The gap is almost always process, not technical difficulty: teams that don't scan at all, or scan but don't act on findings, versus teams that treat a scan failure as a build-blocking gate the same way a failing test would be.

slides.subTitle: Container isolation is not a security boundary by default
slides.markdown:
It's worth being explicit about a subtlety that trips up even experienced engineers: containers share the host machine's kernel — unlike a VM, there's no hardware-level virtualization boundary between a container and the host by default. Container isolation (namespaces, cgroups) is real and does meaningful work, but it was designed primarily for resource and process isolation, not as a hardened security boundary against a determined attacker with code execution inside the container.

This is precisely why **container-breakout** vulnerabilities — bugs that let code inside a container escape to the host — are a recurring, serious category, and why the hardening covered in this topic (non-root, read-only filesystem, minimal images, and never mounting the host's Docker socket into a container, which hands a container direct control over the host's container runtime) matters as much as it does. Treating a container as an unbreakable security sandbox, rather than a convenience-and-isolation mechanism with a real but imperfect boundary, is the conceptual mistake underneath most container-security incidents.

slides.sectionTitle: Mounting the Docker socket into a container
slides.markdown:
The pitfall: mounting the host's Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) into a container — often done to let a CI runner or a monitoring tool spin up sibling containers — without recognizing what that grant actually means. The Docker socket is a direct control channel to the host's container runtime. A container with access to it can create, inspect, or run new containers on the host with privileges of its own choosing, including mounting the host's entire root filesystem into a new container it creates — which is a straightforward, well-documented path to full host compromise, not a theoretical one.

This is a **container-breakout path granted voluntarily**, not a vulnerability that needs to be discovered — the isolation was never violated by an attacker, it was handed away in the deployment configuration. It shows up constantly in "Docker-in-Docker" style CI setups because it's the easy way to let a build job build and run containers, and the security implication is often not obvious to whoever wired it up.

The fix is using a purpose-built, sandboxed alternative for container-in-container workloads (rootless builders like Kaniko or Buildah, or a properly isolated Docker-in-Docker setup that doesn't share the host's socket) rather than mounting the host's own socket directly into a container that doesn't need — and shouldn't have — that level of control over the host.
